content.title: A network with a job
content.text: One of the first jobs a neural network did for money, from 1989: reading handwritten digits on postcodes and cheques. This is a simplified version of that network, with a real picture from the same kind of data. The job is small and clear: look at the picture, say which digit it is.

content.title: A picture is numbers
content.text: To a network a picture is a list of numbers: one per pixel, how bright it is, here from 0 to 16. Eight by eight pixels, 64 numbers. Those are the inputs, the numbers in from the previous pill. No weights yet: this is only the raw data being lined up.

content.title: The rows
content.text: Three rows of neurons: 32, then 16, then 10. Every neuron does the recipe from the previous pill on every number from the row before. The rows get shorter because the network squeezes 64 numbers down to ten answers. The last row has exactly ten neurons because there are ten possible digits.

content.title: The forward pass
content.text: Feed the 64 numbers in and let them flow. On every wire the number is multiplied by that wire’s weight: bright wires carry a lot, dark wires almost nothing, and a dark pixel sends nothing at all. Inside each neuron the arrivals are added, the bias is added, the total is squashed, and one number leaves for the next row. This is the forward pass: just the calculation, done once.

content.title: Ten scores
content.text: The ten outputs are scores, one per digit, adding up to 100%. The biggest is the network’s answer. Here it says 3, and it is right. These scores are real: this network was trained on 3,823 pictures with the same recipe the later pills explain, then shown pictures it had never seen.

content.title: Another picture, and a mistake
content.text: A different picture, the same 2,778 numbers inside, a different answer out: nothing inside changed, only the inputs did. And it can be wrong. The third picture is a 7, and the network says 9, very confidently. On 1,797 unseen pictures it gets 1,724 right, about 96 out of 100.

content.title: Where the knowledge lives
content.text: Everything this network knows is in its 2,778 weights and biases. Before training they were random numbers, and the scores for the same 3 were noise: every digit near 10%. Training nudged every one of those numbers, a little at a time, until the right score came out. How that nudging works is the rest of this series.
